lead: A rigid body is in equilibrium when it does not accelerate: the forces on it cancel and their turning effects also cancel. Written as equations, the sum of all forces is zero and the sum of all moments about any chosen point is zero. In a plane this gives three scalar equations, so a support system with three unknown reactions can be solved. The idea is used everywhere a body must stay put: a beam on a wall, a ladder against a wall, a shelf bracket, or a machine base bolted to a floor.
prereq: You need moments, support reactions, and equivalent force systems, plus equilibrium of a particle from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A rigid body in a plane has three possible motions to stop: sliding along x, sliding along y, and turning in the plane. Equilibrium stops all three. The force equations stop the sliding; the moment equation stops the turning. The conditions are ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0, and ΣM<sub>O</sub> = 0, where x and y are any two perpendicular axes in the plane and O is any point in the plane.

blocks.where: ΣF<sub>x</sub> and ΣF<sub>y</sub> are the sums of force components along the axes, in N; ΣM<sub>O</sub> is the sum of moments about O, in N·m; counterclockwise moments are positive.

blocks.text: The point O is free. A body that is in equilibrium has zero moment about every point, so you may choose whichever point makes the arithmetic easiest. The three equations are not independent for every choice: do not take all three as moment equations about points on one line, because those equations repeat one another. Three moment equations are valid only about three non-collinear points.

Three equations solve at most three unknown reaction components. A roller gives one, a pin gives two, a fixed support gives three. If your free body diagram has four unknowns, the body is statically indeterminate: equilibrium alone cannot find them, and you need compatibility of deformation.

Every problem follows the same order. Draw the free body diagram first. Replace each support by its reaction components, using the support table from types of supports. Include the body's own weight at its centre of gravity. Only then write equations.

items: Draw the free body diagram: isolate the body, show all applied forces and all reactions, and label unknown components.
Choose axes along the most forces to reduce components.
Choose a moment point where one or more unknown forces pass, because their moment is zero there.
Write ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0, and ΣM<sub>O</sub> = 0; solve for the unknowns.
Check with an equation you did not use, such as ΣM about another point.

blocks.text: The moment point is the main labour-saving choice. A force whose line of action passes through O has zero moment about O, so O removes that unknown from the moment equation. In the figure, the recipe puts the moment equation after the force equations, but the order can change: if the force equations would contain two unknowns each, take moments first about a point that kills one of them.

Other valid sets exist. You may replace one force equation by a moment equation about a second point, giving two moment equations and one force equation. You may use three moment equations about three non-collinear points. These sets are equivalent to the first set, not extra equations. A common mistake is to write four equations for three unknowns and treat the fourth as a check; it is a check only if it is independent.

In three dimensions a body can slide along three axes and rotate about three axes. Six equations are needed: ΣF<sub>x</sub>, ΣF<sub>y</sub>, ΣF<sub>z</sub>, and ΣM<sub>x</sub>, ΣM<sub>y</sub>, ΣM<sub>z</sub>, all equal to zero. The force equations stop sliding; the moment equations stop rotation about the axes. Six equations solve at most six unknown reaction components.
ΣF<sub>x</sub> = ΣF<sub>y</sub> = ΣF<sub>z</sub> = 0, ΣM<sub>x</sub> = ΣM<sub>y</sub> = ΣM<sub>z</sub> = 0
blocks.where: the F sums are force components in N along three perpendicular axes; the M sums are moments about those axes in N·m.

blocks.text: The vector form is ΣF = 0 and ΣMO = 0, where F is a force vector and MO is the moment vector about point O. In space, the moment of a force about an axis is found from the component of the moment vector along that axis. A ball-and-socket support gives three force reactions and no moment; a fixed support gives three force and three moment reactions. If there are more than six unknowns, the body is statically indeterminate.

Use the same method: free body diagram, axes, moment point or moment axes that remove unknowns, solve, check. A useful check in space is to take moments about a different point; the moments of all forces about that point must still sum to zero.

figure.caption: The equilibrium recipe for a planar body: the free body diagram feeds the two force equations and one moment equation, and the reactions are solved only if the unknowns do not exceed three.

spec.title: Equilibrium recipe
spec.aria: The equilibrium recipe: draw the free body diagram, write the two force equations and one moment equation in a plane, solve for the reactions and check that the unknowns never exceed three.

examples.question: A massless beam AB of length 3 m is hinged to a wall at A and held by a cable at B. The cable makes 45° with the beam and pulls up and toward the wall. A load of 500 N hangs from the beam at 2 m from A. Find the cable tension and the hinge reaction.
steps: Draw the free body diagram. At the hinge A show A<sub>x</sub> and A<sub>y</sub>. At B show the cable tension T at 45° above the beam, pointing up and toward the wall. At 2 m from A show the 500 N load acting down.
Take x along the beam away from the wall and y upward. The cable has components T cos 45° toward the wall and T sin 45° upward.

Take moments about A. The hinge reactions and the horizontal component of T pass through A, so only T sin 45° and the 500 N load have moments. Counterclockwise is positive: (T sin 45°)(3 m) − (500 N)(2 m) = 0.
ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0: A<sub>x</sub> − T cos 45° = 0, so A<sub>x</sub> = 471.4 × 0.7071 = 333.3 N. The positive sign means A<sub>x</sub> acts away from the wall.
ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0: A<sub>y</sub> + T sin 45° − 500 N = 0, so A<sub>y</sub> = 500 − 333.3 = 166.7 N upward.
examples.answer: The cable tension is 471.4 N, and the hinge reaction is A<sub>x</sub> = 333.3 N away from the wall and A<sub>y</sub> = 166.7 N upward.
examples.check:
import math
T = (2*500)/(3*math.sin(math.radians(45)))
Ax = T*math.cos(math.radians(45))
Ay = 500 - T*math.sin(math.radians(45))
print(round(T, 1))
print(round(Ax, 1))
print(round(Ay, 1))

traps: Dropping a horizontal force applied above the moment point: it still has moment equal to force times perpendicular distance.
Forgetting the body's own weight, or placing the weight at a support instead of at the centre of gravity.
Taking moments about a point that leaves two unknowns in the same equation, then making a sign error while solving.
Treating dependent equations as extra checks: four equations for three unknowns do not make an indeterminate body determinate.
In space, forgetting the moment reaction components at a fixed support and using only the three force equations.

quiz.q: Write the three scalar equilibrium equations for a coplanar rigid body.
quiz.a: ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0, and ΣM<sub>O</sub> = 0, where O is any point in the plane.

quiz.q: Why may the moment point O be chosen anywhere in the plane?
quiz.a: A body in equilibrium has zero moment about every point. Choosing O only changes the bookkeeping, not the physical condition.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries a 600 N load at 1 m from the left support. Find both vertical reactions.
quiz.a: Take moments about the left support: R<sub>R</sub>(4) − 600(1) = 0, so R<sub>R</sub> = 150 N. ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0 gives R<sub>L</sub> = 450 N. Both act upward.

quiz.q: A free body diagram has a pin at A, a roller at B, and an unknown horizontal cable force at C. Can equilibrium find all reactions? Explain.
quiz.a: The pin gives two unknowns, the roller one, and the cable one: four unknowns in total. Plane equilibrium gives only three independent equations, so the body is statically indeterminate by one degree. More information, such as cable stretch, is needed.

quiz.q: How many independent scalar equilibrium equations exist in space? List them.
quiz.a: Six: ΣF<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>y</sub> = 0, ΣF<sub>z</sub> = 0, ΣM<sub>x</sub> = 0, ΣM<sub>y</sub> = 0, ΣM<sub>z</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: A horizontal force of 200 N acts at 2 m above a hinge. Find its moment about the hinge.
quiz.a: Moment = force × perpendicular distance = 200 N × 2 m = 400 N·m about the hinge.

quiz.q: Why are three moment equations about three collinear points not a valid independent set?
quiz.a: For collinear points the three moment equations differ only by a force term common to them, so they are not independent. They cannot supply three separate conditions on three unknown reactions.

quiz.q: What does statically indeterminate mean for a rigid body in equilibrium?
quiz.a: The free body diagram has more unknown reactions than independent equilibrium equations. Equilibrium alone cannot find them; deformation or compatibility conditions must be used.

beyond: Not for the exam. In design offices, statically indeterminate beams are solved with compatibility and stiffness methods; the equilibrium equations here become the first check on any computer frame analysis. Robotics uses the same six equations for a manipulator base: a wrist force sensor measures the six reaction components. Search for 'static equilibrium of a rigid body 3D', 'free body diagram beam hinge cable', and 'statically indeterminate beam compatibility'.
